name: Azerbaijan
summary: A Caspian country rich in oil; briefly independent (1918–20), Soviet, then independent in 1991; regained Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020–23.

knownFor.label: Baku oil
knownFor.note: One of the first oil industries (1800s).

location.value: In the South Caucasus, on the western shore of the Caspian Sea.

terrain.value: The Greater and Lesser Caucasus and Talysh mountains cover about 40% of the land, around central flatlands and the Kura-Aras lowland.

climate.value: Subtropical on most foothills and plains, as the Greater Caucasus blocks cold air from the north.

resources.value: Two-thirds of the country is rich in oil and natural gas.

disasters.value: Nearly half of all the mud volcanoes on Earth are in Azerbaijan; hundreds of earthquake-prediction stations have been built.

urbanisation.value: Baku is the capital and largest city.

migration.value: The Karabakh conflict displaced more than a million people (over 800,000 Azerbaijanis and 300,000 Armenians); many Russians and Armenians left in the 1990s.

economicBase.value: Oil and natural gas; by 2012 GDP had grown 20-fold since 1995.

tradeRoutes.value: The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline (opened May 2006) runs through Georgia to Turkey; the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway also links to Turkey.

moneyAndTax.value: The Azerbaijani manat; a new manat was launched on 1 January 2006.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: Constitutionally a presidential republic; in practice an authoritarian regime whose elections are marred by fraud.

succession.value: Ilham Aliyev became president when his father, Heydar Aliyev, died in 2003.

institutions.value: The President and the 125-member unicameral National Assembly (Milli Majlis).

stability.value: A 1993 military insurrection brought Heydar Aliyev to power and a 1994 coup attempt failed; the government is criticised for media restrictions and repression.

eliteConflict.value: In 1993 a military insurrection led by Surat Huseynov overthrew the elected president, Abulfaz Elchibey.

armyAndTech.value: Arms imports mainly from Russia (about 85% in one report); also from Israel, Turkey and Belarus.
armyAndTech.source: Eurasianet: Azerbaijan gets 85 percent of its weapons from Russia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

majorWars.value: The First Nagorno-Karabakh War (ended 1994), the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War (2020) and an Azerbaijani offensive in 2023.

territoryChange.value: After the 2020 war the seven districts and parts of Nagorno-Karabakh were returned to Azerbaijani control; a 2023 offensive ended the Republic of Artsakh.

alliancesRivals.value: A "special relationship" with Turkey; an active member of the Organization of Turkic States.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Oil and gas pipelines to Turkey and Europe, and the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway.

religion.value: About 97% Muslim, an estimated 55–65% of them Shia; the constitution declares no official religion.

languageWriting.value: Azerbaijani, a Turkic language, written in a modified Latin alphabet that replaced Cyrillic after independence.

artsArchitecture.value: The Walled City of Baku, with the Maiden Tower and the Palace of the Shirvanshahs.

socialStructure.value: 94.8% Azerbaijanis in the 2019 census, with small Lezgin, Talysh and Russian minorities.

sharedIdentity.value: One of six independent Turkic states; an Azerbaijani national identity emerged in the late 19th century.

dailyLife.value: Saffron-rice plov is the flagship dish, and black tea the national drink.

neighbours.value: Russia, Georgia, Armenia, Iran and Turkey (via the Nakhchivan exclave).

ideasReligions.value: Considered the most secular Muslim-majority country.

colonisation.value: Ceded to the Russian Empire by Iran (1813 and 1828); part of the Soviet Union from 1920 until 1991.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
